question: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of difficulty initiating urination. He wakes up at least 3–4 times at night to urinate. Digital rectal examination shows a symmetrically enlarged, nontender prostate with a rubbery consistency. Laboratory studies show a prostate-specific antigen level of 2.1 ng/mL (N < 4). Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?

options.opa: Hyperplasia of lateral prostatic lobe tissue
options.opc: Hypertrophy of middle prostatic lobe tissue
options.opd: Lymphocytic infiltration of anterior prostatic lobe stroma
options.ope: Infiltrating dysplasia of posterior prostatic lobe epithelium

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Hypertrophy of middle prostatic lobe tissue -> Difficulty initiating urination -> Waking up multiple times at night to urinate -> Symmetrically enlarged prostate on digital rectal examination -> Rubber consistency of the prostate -> Most likely underlying cause of the patient's symptoms -> 95%
enhanced_information: The most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms is hypertrophy of middle prostatic lobe tissue, leading to difficulty initiating urination, frequent nighttime urination, symmetrically enlarged prostate with a rubbery consistency. The evidence path of rectal examination causing pain via paracrine processes in the prostate is not directly relevant to the key point.
analysis: The patient's symptoms of difficulty initiating urination, frequent nighttime urination, and an enlarged, rubbery prostate with a PSA level within normal range are indicative of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). BPH commonly involves the middle prostatic lobe, leading to obstruction of the urethra and subsequent urinary symptoms. The digital rectal examination findings of symmetrically enlarged, nontender prostate further support the diagnosis of BPH.
